## Overall Research Question

The goal of this project was to investigate how quickly the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal for different types of populations. The project also examined what happens when the assumptions of the usual Central Limit Theorem are questionable or fail.

## How Approximate Normality Was Judged

I used several forms of evidence rather than relying on one rule or only visually inspecting the graphs. For each sample size, I examined the histogram, normal Q-Q plot, skewness, excess kurtosis, simulated mean, theoretical mean, simulated standard error, theoretical standard error, and the ratio of simulated to theoretical standard error. I selected the smallest sample size for which the graphical and numerical evidence were reasonably consistent with approximate normality.

## Required-Distribution Results

| Population | Selected n | Theoretical mean | Theoretical SD | Simulated mean | Mean error | Simulated SE | Theoretical SE | SE ratio | Skewness | Excess kurtosis | Normality evidence / conclusion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Standard Normal | 1 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 | -0.0055 | 0.0055 | 1.0069 | 1.0000 | 1.0069 | -0.0181 | 0.0368 | Approximately normal immediately; histogram and Q-Q plot are consistent with normality |
| Six-Sided Die | 30 | 3.5000 | 1.7078 | 3.5020 | 0.0020 | 0.3168 | 0.3117 | 1.0164 | 0.0203 | 0.0049 | Bounded and symmetric; sampling distribution is approximately normal at n = 30 |
| Exponential | 30 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0013 | 0.0013 | 0.1827 | 0.1826 | 1.0007 | 0.3581 | 0.1738 | Right-skew is reduced substantially; approximate normality is reasonable at n = 30 |
| Small Binomial | 30 | 0.5000 | 0.6708 | 0.5004 | 0.0004 | 0.1233 | 0.1225 | 1.0065 | 0.2141 | 0.0222 | Skewness and discreteness are reduced; approximate normality is reasonable at n = 30 |
| Cauchy | Not applicable | Undefined | Undefined | Unstable | Unstable | Unstable | Undefined | Not applicable | Unstable | Unstable | No ordinary CLT cutoff; the Cauchy distribution has no finite mean or variance |

The standard normal population was approximately normal immediately because the original population was already normal. The die, exponential, and small binomial populations required larger sample sizes because they were discrete or skewed. The Cauchy population did not produce a stable approximately normal sampling distribution because it does not have a finite ordinary mean or variance.

## Extra-Credit Results

| Population | Selected n | Main conclusion |
|---|---:|---|
| Dependent Machine Failure | 200 | Dependence slows convergence toward normality |
| Non-Identical Bernoulli | 30 | Approximate normality is reasonable when the adjusted SE is used |
| Custom Life/Death Population | 30 | The irregular population shape becomes less influential as n increases |

The dependent machine-failure process required a larger sample size because each observation was influenced by the previous one. The non-identical Bernoulli process became approximately normal at a smaller sample size when the changing success probabilities were included in the theoretical variance calculation. The custom life/death population became smoother and more symmetric as the sample size increased.

## Is n = 30 a Universal Rule?

The final results do not support treating n = 30 as a universal guarantee. It is a useful rule of thumb for several finite-mean and finite-variance populations, but the speed of convergence depends on the original population. The standard normal population was approximately normal at n = 1, while the die, exponential, small binomial, and custom life/death populations required larger sample sizes. The dependent machine-failure process required an even larger sample size because the observations were not independent. The Cauchy case was an important exception because increasing n did not overcome the lack of a finite mean and variance.

## Which Populations Converged Fastest and Slowest?

The standard normal population converged immediately because it was already normally distributed. The six-sided die population also converged relatively quickly because it was symmetric and bounded, although it remained discrete at smaller sample sizes. The exponential and small binomial populations converged more gradually because they were right-skewed. The custom life/death population also required additional sample size because it had an irregular and asymmetric shape. The dependent machine-failure process converged more slowly because observations influenced one another. The Cauchy population did not converge to an ordinary normal sampling distribution because extreme values continued to affect the sample mean. Within the displayed range, its histograms remained broadly similar across sample sizes, while the numerical results showed that its mean and tail behavior remained unstable.

## What Happened When CLT Assumptions Were Violated?

The Cauchy experiment showed that simply increasing the sample size does not always make sample averages look normally distributed. Because the Cauchy distribution can produce extremely large values, a few unusual observations can continue to strongly affect the average, even when many observations are included. The dependent machine-failure experiment showed that observations cannot always be treated as unrelated because one failure time can influence the next failure time. This dependence slows the process of becoming approximately normal and makes the usual independent-observation reasoning less direct. The non-identical Bernoulli experiment showed that observations do not always need to follow exactly the same distribution. However, when the probability of success changes from one observation to the next, those changing probabilities must be included when calculating the expected variation in the sample averages. Together, these examples show that the Central Limit Theorem is useful, but its conclusions depend on the type of data being analyzed and the assumptions made about the observations.

## Reproducibility

The simulations use a seed based on the last four digits of my student ID so that the random results can be reproduced. Using a seed does not prevent unusual results or guarantee that the simulation is unbiased. Instead, it ensures that the same code produces the same random samples each time it is run. When one experiment is rerun with a different seed, the exact simulated means, standard errors, and shape statistics may change slightly, but the overall conclusions should remain similar. This shows that the conclusions are based on the general simulation pattern rather than one particular random sample.

## Final Takeaway

The simulations showed that there is no single sample size that works equally well for every population. The standard normal population was approximately normal at n = 1, while the die, exponential, small binomial, and custom life/death populations generally required around n = 30. The dependent machine-failure process required a larger sample size because observations influenced one another, while the non-identical Bernoulli process became approximately normal at n = 30 when its changing probabilities were included in the calculations. The Cauchy population did not become stable because extreme values continued to affect the sample mean. Overall, the results show that the appropriate sample size depends on the data-generating process, so decisions should be based on the observed simulations and diagnostics rather than automatically using n = 30.
